accent.settles: lists three accents: acute, circumflex and grave.
accent.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 1: Grammar

accusative.note: Huffman's accusative is "the case of extent or limits on the verb's action"; the definition named only the direct object, and now names extent too.
accusative.settles: gives the accusative as the case of extent or of limits on the verb's action, the direct object being its first use.
accusative.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 2: Syntax

active.settles: gives the active as the subject activating the action.
active.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 2: Syntax

adjective.note: agreement in case, gender and number is in every grammar; the rest is ordinary English.

anarthrous.note: θεός is Huffman's own illustration of it.
anarthrous.settles: discusses a noun without the article, using θεός as the illustration and distinguishing indefinite, definite and qualitative senses.
anarthrous.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 2: Syntax

antecedent.note: The app uses it of any pronoun pointing back — ἐκεῖνος agreeing with ὁ παράκλητος in chapter 11 — so "relative pronoun" was too narrow. Note Black uses the word in a different sense again, of antecedent ACTION.
antecedent.settles: uses the word in a different sense again — of antecedent ACTION, a participle acting before the main verb — which is worth knowing when reading him.
antecedent.source: Black, Learn to Read NT Greek, lesson 20

aorist.settles: gives the aorist as viewing the action as a whole, with remoteness that is often but not always temporal.
aorist.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 2: Syntax

apodosis.settles: names the two halves of a conditional: the protasis is the if, the apodosis the then.
apodosis.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 2: Syntax

article.settles: states that Greek has a definite article and no indefinite one.
article.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 2: Syntax

aspect.settles: sets out three aspects an author chooses between, and names the tense-forms that carry each.
aspect.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 2: Syntax

athematic.note: Neither Huffman nor Black uses the word — both say "-μι conjugation" instead. The substance is theirs: Huffman gives the connecting vowel as a slot the ω-verbs fill, and the μι-verbs are the ones that do not.

attendant circumstance.settles: defines the participle of attendant circumstance as expressing an action accompanying the main verb, translatable with “and” plus a finite verb.
attendant circumstance.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 2: Syntax

attributive.settles: defines the attributive adjective as attributing a quality to its noun, standing inside the article group.
attributive.source: Black, Learn to Read NT Greek, lesson 6

augment.note: Huffman confirms the restriction the definition makes: the augment is indicative mood only.
augment.settles: restricts the augment to the imperfect, aorist and pluperfect, and to the indicative mood only, with lengthening where the verb begins with a vowel.
augment.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 1: Grammar

breathing.note: Huffman: "words beginning with a vowel (or ρ)". The definition had vowels alone; initial ρ takes a rough breathing too.
breathing.settles: puts the breathing mark on words beginning with a vowel or with ρ, rough adding an h and smooth adding nothing.
breathing.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 1: Grammar

case.settles: describes the case ending as a flag for the role a noun plays in its sentence.
case.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 2: Syntax

conjugation.note: Black uses the word for the FAMILY of a verb as well as the act of running one through — the -ω and -μι conjugations — which is what the declension entry already said about nouns.
conjugation.settles: divides Greek verbs into two conjugations, the -ω verbs and the -μι verbs.
conjugation.source: Black, Learn to Read NT Greek, lesson 18-19

contract verb.note: Black names the vowels: a SHORT α, ε or ο. The definition said only "a vowel".
contract verb.settles: defines a contract verb as one whose stem ends in a short α, ε or ο.
contract verb.source: Black, Learn to Read NT Greek, lesson 18-19

dative.settles: gives the dative as the case of personal interest, typically naming to or for whom something is done.
dative.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 2: Syntax

declension.settles: describes three groupings of nouns, called declensions, each with its own case spellings.
declension.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 1: Grammar

deponent.note: Huffman's wording is the definition's almost exactly.
deponent.settles: defines deponent verbs as middle or passive in form with active meaning, arising where a verb lacks active endings.
deponent.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 1: Grammar

distributive.note: Robertson for the category; the app's own chapter 8 supplies the example, ἀνὰ δύο.
distributive.settles: treats the distributive use, of the by-the-day and twice-a-week kind.

enclitic.settles: defines an enclitic as a word that regularly loses its accent to the word before it, and a proclitic as one that loses it to the word after.
enclitic.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 1: Grammar

ending.note: ordinary grammatical English; Huffman's "the case ending is a function flag" says the same thing about nouns.

feminine.note: one of the three genders; no claim beyond that.

future.note: The definition gave time alone. Huffman groups the future with the aorist under summary aspect but flags the debate, so the definition now says which half is dependable.
future.settles: groups the future with the aorist under summary aspect, while noting that the future's aspect is disputed among scholars.
future.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 2: Syntax

genitive.settles: gives the genitive as the most flexible of case, generally describing the noun it follows.
genitive.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 2: Syntax

genitive absolute.note: Huffman: "the subject of the participle's action is also in the genitive", and his example is a PRONOUN, αὐτοῦ. "A participle and a noun" was too narrow.
genitive absolute.settles: defines it as an anarthrous genitive participle in a phrase with no grammatical tie to the rest of the sentence, the participle's own subject also genitive.
genitive absolute.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 2: Syntax

imperative.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 2: Syntax

imperfect.settles: gives the imperfect as viewing the action as a process, with remoteness that is usually past.
imperfect.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 2: Syntax

imperfective.note: Present and Imperfect, which is what the definition says.
imperfective.settles: assigns the present and the imperfect to the imperfective aspect, which views an action as a process.
imperfective.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 2: Syntax

indicative.settles: assigns actuality to the indicative — the author's portrayal, he is careful to say, not necessarily the fact.
indicative.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 2: Syntax

infinitive.note: Black pairs them: the participle is a verbal adjective, the infinitive a verbal noun. The definition omitted the noun half, which is also what chapter 22's own title says.
infinitive.settles: pairs the two hybrids: the participle is a verbal adjective and the infinitive a verbal noun.
infinitive.source: Black, Learn to Read NT Greek, lesson 21-22

interjection.settles: treats ἰδού and ἴδε as interjections, with οὐαί as another.
interjection.source: Black, Learn to Read NT Greek, lesson 23-24

liquid verb.settles: lists the liquid consonants as λ, μ, ν and ρ.
liquid verb.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 1: Grammar

masculine.note: one of the three genders; no claim beyond that.

middle.settles: gives the middle as the subject both activating and receiving the action.
middle.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 2: Syntax

mood.note: Huffman puts POTENTIALITY under the subjunctive and INTENTION under the imperative. The definition had "supposing or intending" together under the subjunctive.
mood.settles: distributes the four moods as actuality, potentiality, possibility and intention — intention belonging to the imperative.
mood.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 2: Syntax

neuter.note: Huffman confirms the claim the definition makes, that nominative and accusative are the same.
neuter.settles: states that neuter nominative and accusative spellings are the same, in the singular and in the plural.
neuter.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 1: Grammar

nominative.note: The same passage lists all five cases and what each does.
nominative.settles: lists the five cases and what each one does.
nominative.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 1: Grammar

optative.note: Huffman's "less than 70" against the 68 counted in the corpus.
optative.settles: puts the optative at fewer than seventy occurrences in the New Testament and names οι or αι as its connecting vowel, ει in the aorist passive.
optative.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 1: Grammar

paradigm.note: ordinary grammatical English, and the app's own chapter 3 introduces it the same way.

participle.settles: calls the participle a verbal adjective, against the infinitive as verbal noun.
participle.source: Black, Learn to Read NT Greek, lesson 21-22

passive.settles: gives the passive as the subject receiving the action.
passive.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 2: Syntax

perfect.settles: gives the perfect as viewing the action as a state, with the emphasis on results that continue.
perfect.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 2: Syntax

perfective.note: Huffman's summary/perfective aspect is carried by the Aorist AND the Future. The definition named the aorist alone.
perfective.settles: assigns the aorist and the future to the summary or perfective aspect, which views an action as a whole.
perfective.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 2: Syntax

pluperfect.settles: assigns the pluperfect to the stative aspect, viewing a state with remoteness.
pluperfect.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 2: Syntax

predicate.settles: defines the predicate position as the adjective standing outside the article group and asserting something of the noun.
predicate.source: Black, Learn to Read NT Greek, lesson 6

principal parts.settles: lists the six principal parts and explains them as a way of holding the key spelling changes.
principal parts.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 1: Grammar

protasis.settles: names the if half of a conditional the protasis.
protasis.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 2: Syntax

reduplication.note: Two faults. Huffman has reduplication building the perfect AND the pluperfect, and the definition named the perfect alone; and it said the ε goes "in front", when γέγραπται puts it after the copied consonant.
reduplication.settles: assigns reduplication to the perfect and pluperfect, and sets out what happens to verbs beginning with a vowel or an awkward consonant.
reduplication.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 1: Grammar

relative pronoun.note: ordinary grammatical English; what is Greek-specific about it lives in the app's own relative-pronoun table.

stative.note: Huffman's stative aspect is carried by the Perfect AND the Pluperfect. The definition named the perfect alone.
stative.settles: assigns the perfect and the pluperfect to the stative aspect, which views the action as a state.
stative.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 2: Syntax

stem.note: ordinary grammatical English; Huffman's "Verb Stem: the foundational core of the verb" is the same.

subjunctive.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 2: Syntax

substantival.note: Huffman's "turn another part of speech into a noun", with οἱ πτωχοί as the example.
substantival.settles: treats the article's power to turn another part of speech into a noun, adjectives and participles included.
substantival.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 2: Syntax

tense.note: Huffman writes "tense-form" throughout for the reason the definition gives.
tense.settles: writes tense-form throughout, and sets the six out by aspect rather than by time.
tense.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 2: Syntax

unmarked.note: a description of emphasis, not a rule of Greek.

vocative.note: Huffman adds what the app's own vocative table found in the corpus: the nominative spelling is often used instead.
vocative.settles: calls it the case of address and notes that the nominative spelling is often used instead.
vocative.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 1: Grammar

voice.settles: describes voice as the subject's relation to the action: doing it, receiving it, or both.
voice.source: Huffman, The Handy Guide to NT Greek, Part 2: Syntax
